opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was back when I was in India, still an undergrad. I wasn't really a "vision person" at all; I was just a kid who liked programming and hacking on stuff. Then I saw the Photosynth demo, the one where they took a pile of ordinary photos people had taken of some landmark and stitched them into a 3D space you could fly through. It just blew my mind.

What got me was that it wasn't using special cameras or a lab setup. It was random photos from different people, different angles, different lighting, and somehow the software figured out how they related to each other in 3D. I remember thinking, "How is that even possible? How does a computer look at a bunch of pixels and understand that it's the same building?" It felt like magic, and I wanted to know how the magic worked.

So I started digging in. I learned about feature matching, structure from motion, all that classical vision stuff, mostly by reading whatever I could find online. That curiosity is what pushed me toward computer vision, and eventually toward grad school in the US. Honestly, I wasn't a great student on paper. I applied to a bunch of places and got rejected from most of them. But that demo gave me a direction I really cared about, and that carried me through a lot of the early rejections and struggles.

In hindsight it's funny. The thing that pulled me in was very geometric, classical vision, and within a few years the whole field had shifted toward deep learning. But the core question, how you get a machine to make sense of the visual world, is the same one I've been chasing ever since.

r001.rationale: The candidate wonders how a computer can understand a building from pixels, but does not describe an attempt to match images by comparing them pixel by pixel.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I have to go back a bit for this. I was in undergrad in India, and honestly I wasn't that interested in computer vision as a field yet. I was more of a general programmer, just hacking on things. And then I saw this Photosynth demo, I think it was the TED talk, where they took a bunch of random photos of Notre Dame that people had uploaded to Flickr, and they reconstructed the whole cathedral in 3D. You could fly around it, zoom into someone's vacation snapshot, and it would seamlessly place it in the scene.

And what got me was that it felt like magic, but it wasn't magic. It was math. It was feature matching, structure from motion, bundle adjustment, all this stuff I had no idea about. The photos were messy, taken by different people with different cameras at different times, and the system just made sense of it. That was the thing that clicked for me: computers could actually understand the world through images, not just store and display them.

So I went and found Noah Snavely's paper, and tried to read it, and understood maybe a third of it. But that was enough. I started playing with OpenCV, doing SIFT features, trying to replicate pieces of it, badly. And that sort of snowballed. One thing led to another and I ended up working on vision full time. I think if you'd asked me before that demo, I would have said I'd do systems or something. That one demo sort of rerouted my whole trajectory.

r001.rationale: The response says Photosynth used feature matching, structure from motion, and bundle adjustment, and mentions trying SIFT with OpenCV. It does not describe an initial pixel-by-pixel comparison approach.

astra-6.text: What struck me was that you could take a bunch of ordinary photographs and use them to reconstruct a place in 3D. You could move through the scene, and the computer had figured out how those images fit together. That felt like magic to me. I wanted to understand how you could get that much information out of pixels, and that curiosity drew me into computer vision.

r001.rationale: The response says he wanted to understand how Photosynth fit images together and extracted information from pixels, but it does not describe an initial attempt framed as pixel-by-pixel comparison.
